questions.stem: Which two quantities does the Ar equation combine for each isotope?

options.text: Percentage abundance and mass number
options.explanation: Each isotope contributes its abundance times its mass, and the terms are then summed.

options.text: Atomic number and charge
options.explanation: Neither appears in the equation; it works purely from masses and abundances.
options.misconception: wrong quantities drafted into the equation

options.text: Electron count and shell number
options.explanation: Electrons are irrelevant here; only the nuclei's masses are being averaged.

options.text: Percentage abundance and atomic number
options.explanation: Abundance pairs with mass number; atomic number never enters the average.
options.misconception: mass number swapped for atomic number

questions.stem: Why is the summed total divided by 100?

options.text: Abundances are percentages, so dividing by 100 turns the weighted sum into the per-atom average
options.explanation: The 100 undoes the percentage scaling so the answer sits on the mass-number scale.

options.text: Because every element has exactly 100 isotopes
options.explanation: Element isotope counts vary; the 100 comes from percentages, not from isotope tallies.

options.text: To cancel the units of mass
options.explanation: Relative masses are unitless comparisons; the division is about percentage scaling.
options.misconception: unit cancellation invented as the reason

options.text: To round the answer to one decimal place
options.explanation: Rounding happens at the end if the question asks; the division computes the true average.

questions.stem: An element turns out to have three isotopes. How does the equation change?

options.text: The top line gains a third term - percentage times mass - while the divisor stays 100
options.explanation: Each extra isotope extends the numerator; the percentage scaling is unchanged.

options.text: The divisor becomes 300
options.explanation: The 100 belongs to the percentage scale, whatever the isotope count.

options.text: The two lightest isotopes are averaged first
options.explanation: All isotopes enter one sum; no stepwise pairing happens.

options.text: The equation cannot cope and Ar is left unknown
options.explanation: The top line is explicitly extendable to any number of isotopes.
options.misconception: equation assumed fixed at two terms

questions.stem: Why is an element's Ar so rarely a whole number?

options.text: It is a weighted average of isotope mass numbers, so it usually lands between them
options.explanation: Unless one isotope dominates almost completely, the blend falls between whole masses.

options.text: Because electron masses add odd fractions
options.explanation: Electron mass is negligible; the blending of isotope masses is the real cause.

options.text: Because instruments cannot measure mass precisely
options.explanation: The non-whole value is mathematical, not a measurement limitation.

options.text: Because mass numbers themselves are averages
options.explanation: Each isotope's mass number is a whole count; the averaging happens across isotopes.

questions.stem: Copper's two stable isotopes are written with 63 and 65 over its symbol. What do those numbers mean?

options.text: Their mass numbers - same element, different neutron counts
options.explanation: The shared symbol fixes the element; the differing top number distinguishes the isotopes.

options.text: Their atomic numbers
options.explanation: Atomic number is fixed for the element; it could not differ between two atoms of copper.
options.misconception: mass number read as atomic number

options.text: Their charges
options.explanation: Charge is written separately and depends on electrons, not on these labels.

options.text: The years they were discovered
options.explanation: Isotope labels are nuclear counts, not dates.

questions.stem: State the term each isotope contributes to the relative-atomic-mass equation.
questions.modelAnswer: Percentage abundance times mass number — each isotope contributes one term.

questions.stem: State where an element's Ar value sits relative to its isotope mass numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: In between — Ar is a weighted average, so it sits between the isotope mass numbers.

questions.stem: Explain why the relative-atomic-mass equation divides the summed terms by 100.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the abundances are percentages — dividing by 100 converts the percentage-weighted total back to an average per atom.

questions.stem: Chlorine has two stable isotopes: 75% of mass 35 and 25% of mass 37. State the top line of the Ar calculation for chlorine.
questions.modelAnswer: (75 x 35) + (25 x 37) — each isotope contributes one term of percentage abundance times mass number.

questions.stem: Rubidium: 72% of mass 85, 28% of mass 87. What is the first working step?

options.text: Multiply each percentage by its own mass number
options.explanation: The two products 72 x 85 and 28 x 87 form the terms that get summed next.

options.text: Add the two percentages together
options.explanation: The percentages already total 100; adding them again is meaningless here.

options.text: Divide both masses by 100
options.explanation: The division by 100 comes once, after the weighted sum, not to each mass.

options.text: Subtract the smaller percentage from the larger
options.explanation: Nothing in the method subtracts; every isotope contributes positively.
6120 plus 2436 lands on 8556, the weighted sum before scaling.
That adds the mass numbers and percentages in a tangle instead of multiplying within each term.
That is only the first product; the second isotope still has to be added in.
That multiplies the two products together rather than adding them.

questions.stem: What does dividing 8556 by 100 give, before rounding?

options.explanation: The full-precision average keeps the digits needed for a correct final round.
85.6 is the rounded answer; the division itself yields 85.56.
options.misconception: rounding applied before it is asked

options.explanation: That shifts a decimal place too far; the divisor is 100, not 1000.
That looks like dividing by 10; the percentage scale divides by 100.

questions.stem: How should 85.56 be reported when the question says one decimal place?

options.text: 85.6, rounding the second decimal up
options.explanation: The .06 remainder pushes the first decimal from 5 to 6.

options.text: 85.5, dropping everything after the first decimal
options.explanation: Truncation is not rounding; the .06 part still moves the digit.

options.text: 86, rounding to the nearest whole number
options.explanation: That answers to zero decimal places; the question asked for one.

options.text: 85.56, decimals kept as they are
options.explanation: The full value is correct working but ignores the requested format.

questions.stem: A different rubidium sample held 50% of each isotope. What Ar would it have?

options.text: 86.0, the plain midpoint of 85 and 87
options.explanation: Equal weights cancel the bias, so the average lands exactly between the masses.

options.text: 85.6, the same as before
options.explanation: That value belongs to the 72-28 split; equal shares shift the average.

options.text: 85, the lighter isotope winning
options.explanation: With equal shares no isotope can dominate the average.

options.text: 172, the mass numbers added
options.explanation: Mass numbers are never simply added; the average stays on their scale.

questions.stem: State the rounding rule of record for relative-atomic-mass working.
questions.modelAnswer: Keep full precision through the working and round only in the final line.

questions.stem: State the two products added in the rubidium top line, and their sum.
Explain why the rubidium sample's Ar (85.6) sits closer to 85 than to 87.
questions.modelAnswer: Because Ar is a weighted average — the 72% abundance of the mass-85 isotope outweighs the 28% of mass-87, so the average sits between the mass numbers but nearer the more abundant isotope.

questions.stem: A different rubidium-like sample holds 60% of mass 85 and 40% of mass 87. Predict whether its Ar sits above or below 86.0.
questions.modelAnswer: Below 86.0 — more of the lighter isotope (60% of mass 85) pulls the weighted average below the 50-50 midpoint of 86.0.
